name: Autoplay audio and video
plain: Starts video or sound automatically; muted video is allowed, sound usually needs prior interaction.
meaning: A site can start media without a click. Browsers allow silent autoplay but block surprise sound unless the person has engaged with the site, which shapes ad video and background audio.

web.api: <video autoplay muted playsinline>; HTMLMediaElement.play(); allow="autoplay"; navigator.getAutoplayPolicy()

access.persistence: Chrome Media Engagement Index (MEI) score is stored per origin
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Top frame must delegate with allow="autoplay" for cross-origin iframes
steps: Element has muted attribute or origin has activation or high MEI
play() resolves or rejects with NotAllowedError
Handle the rejection and show a play button

limits.headline: Can start muted video on its own, and sound only after you have interacted
limits.user_action: Nothing for muted video. For sound, you tap, click or press a key on the site first
can: Start a silent video without a click
Start sound after you have clicked, tapped or watched on the site
Start a clip after you tap Play
cannot: Play sound on a first visit without any interaction
Keep a sound ad alive in a tab you muted
Play a video in the background once the page is hidden on most phones
limits.reach_label: Muted video, sound after you interact
limits.differs: Safari and iPhone are strict about sound. Chrome and Edge allow sound for sites you used often. Firefox lets you block it.

story.what_it_is: A page can start video or sound by itself. Muted video is usually fine, sound needs your action first.

marketing.name: Autoplay policy
marketing.pitch: Chrome allows muted autoplay, and lets sound autoplay only after you have interacted with the site.

marketing.name: New video policies for iOS
marketing.pitch: Safari lets muted videos play inline automatically, and requires a tap for videos with sound.

story.for_you: A video on a page may start playing silently as you scroll. Sound normally starts only after you click or tap. Browsers keep this rule to avoid surprise noise.
story.for_makers: Makers use muted autoplay to show previews and grab attention, which raises views and ad time. They ask for a tap before sound. Games need one click before audio. Ads that autoplay can annoy users.

use_cases.example: A streaming home page plays a silent trailer behind the title, so browsing feels alive.
A browser game must wait for your first click or key press before its music and sounds can play.
A social feed starts muted clips as you scroll, and you tap to hear them.
A news site starts a muted video in an article, which many people watch with captions.
A video ad starts muted in the page, and counts a view after a few seconds.
A store plays a muted product video on the page to show the item in use.
A live stream page starts muted and asks you to unmute for sound.
A music site shows a play button, because the browser blocks sound until you tap.

technical_bounds: Muted autoplay is allowed everywhere (iOS also needs playsinline)
Chrome 66: audible autoplay needs user activation on the origin, a high MEI score, or an installed PWA; MEI needs roughly 20 visits and a score of about 0.2 to 0.3 (Chromium source)
MEI counts a play as significant when media plays 7 s or more, is audible, tab active, and video at least 200 by 140 px
Firefox 66 blocks audible autoplay by default (site exceptions allowed); Safari 11 on macOS and iOS 10 block audible autoplay by default
Chrome mutes autoplay in cross-origin iframes unless allow="autoplay" is set

history.change: Block audible autoplay by default on macOS
Autoplay policy: muted allowed; audible needs activation, MEI or PWA
Autoplay policy for media in background tabs unchanged; play() promise rejection documented widely
